summary: This ACS news note reports a study showing that compostable food containers, which often use PFAS to repel water and oil, can leach these chemicals into compost. Researchers led by Linda Lee analyzed 10 compost samples from five U.S. states and found PFAAs in all of them, with higher totals at facilities that accepted compostable food packaging. Most detected compounds were short-chain PFAAs, and the health effects of applying such compost to crops remain unknown. The study helped inform Washington State's 2018 Healthy Food Packaging Act banning PFAS in paper food packaging after January 1, 2022.
one_line: A study finds PFAS chemicals from compostable food containers leach into compost, with unknown effects on crops and health.
key_facts: Compostable food containers often rely on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) to repel water and oil.
Researchers reported in ACS' Environmental Science & Technology Letters that PFAS can leach from compostable containers into compost.
Two long-chain PFAS, perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS), have been linked to negative health effects.
Companies in the U.S. voluntarily phased out production of PFOA and PFOS, and many manufacturers switched to shorter-chain PFAS.
Previous research showed PFAS in biosolids applied as fertilizer can migrate from soil to plants and accumulate in humans through the food chain.
Linda Lee and colleagues obtained 10 compost samples from five states: nine from commercial facilities and one from a backyard compost bin.
The researchers extracted perfluoroalkyl acids (PFAAs), compounds produced by microbial degradation of PFAS during composting, and analyzed them using mass spectrometry.
Samples from seven facilities that accepted compostable food packaging had higher total PFAA levels than the two that did not or the backyard bin, which contained no food packaging.
PFAAs corresponding to PFOA and PFOS were found in all samples, but most detected compounds were short-chain PFAAs.
The study's results contributed to the 2018 passage of Washington State's Healthy Food Packaging Act.
The Healthy Food Packaging Act will ban the use of PFAS in paper food packaging after January 1, 2022.
